overview.text: Natural selection is an evolutionary process in which inherited differences among individuals affect how many descendants they leave. When a trait gives an advantage in a particular environment, individuals carrying it tend, on average, to survive and reproduce more, so the trait may become more common over generations; selection acts on individuals, while populations change. It requires heritable variation and does not mean organisms change because they need to, or that the “fittest” are necessarily strongest. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the idea and presented it jointly in 1858; Darwin expanded it in On the Origin of Species (1859). Finches studied over generations show selection as environmental conditions shift.

key_facts.text: Natural selection needs heritable variation in a population; differences caused only by non-genetic factors will not be passed on as an evolutionary change.
An advantage depends on the environment, and evolutionary fitness is about contributing offspring to later generations—not simply being strong or surviving.
Individuals are affected by selection; over generations, the frequencies of inherited traits change in populations.
Darwin and Wallace independently developed the idea and presented their work on natural selection together in 1858.
Studies of Galápagos finches documented shifts in average beak size associated with changing food availability, illustrating selection across generations.
